coverage: The Capacity Building Training Programme on GDDP/GMDP for Nandyal district was conducted on 01 August 2026 through in-person departmental interaction sessions. A five-member team engaged district officials across Primary, Secondary and Tertiary sector departments to capture sector-wise field observations, ongoing programmes, implementation status, systemic constraints and key recommendations, in line with the Swarna Andhra @ 2047 District Economic Profiling framework.

highlights.head: Primary Sector
points: Despite abundant irrigation, fertile soils and high productivity, agriculture remains heavily dependent on paddy mono- cropping, limiting crop diversification and income growth.

The district produces substantial agricultural and horticultural output, but weak post-harvest infrastructure (cold storage, processing units, drying platforms and value addition) results in significant losses and lower farmer incomes.

Natural resources provide strong growth potential—high-value horticulture, dairy, inland fisheries and forest-based livelihoods—but productivity is constrained by quality inputs (seed, feed), climate risks and weak market linkages.

highlights.head: Secondary Sector
points: Nandyal possesses abundant limestone and mineral resources with an established cement industry, yet downstream mineral-based manufacturing and value addition remain underdeveloped.

Industrial growth is constrained less by resource availability and more by ecosystem gaps such as lack of plug-and- play industrial parks, expensive land, limited access to finance and industry-ready skills.

The district has significant opportunities in agro-processing, biomass utilisation and renewable energy (solar, wind and hydro), but these sectors require stronger infrastructure and private investment.

highlights.head: Tertiary Sector
points: Tourism has high visitor inflows and diverse attractions, but inadequate accommodation, transport connectivity and visitor amenities prevent longer tourist stays and higher local spending.
Human capital is improving through education and skill programmes, yet graduates continue to migrate due to limited local employment opportunities and weak industry-academia linkages.

Financial and service-sector expansion is constrained by limited credit access (collateral requirements), insufficient specialised healthcare facilities and transport infrastructure gaps, despite improving public service delivery.

coverage: The Capacity Building Training Programme on GDDP/GCDP/GMDP for Nandyal district was conducted as a full-day, highly interactive, in- person session under the Swarna Andhra @ 2047 initiative, delivered by the Pahle India Foundation (PIF) for District HODs, CSOs and MSOs. The Capacity Building Programme was graced by the presence of District Collector Smt. Rajakumari Ganiya, Director of Economics and Statistics Sri B. Gopal (Vijayawada), District Economics and Statistics Officer (CPO), Nandyal, Sri K. Prakash, and Deputy Statistical Officer, Directorate of Economics and Statistics, Vijayawada, Sri Chandrashekhar, whose participation added valuable insights and guidance to the programme. The programme was inaugurated by District Collector Smt. Rajakumari Ganiya, who spoke about the importance of the initiative in supporting the district's long-term development. She encouraged all participants to actively engage in the sessions and make the most of the opportunity to learn and contribute. Following the inaugural address, Mr. Rahees provided an overview of the day's programme and explained the structure of the training. The Director of the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES), Sri. B. Gopal then addressed the participants, highlighting the importance of the programme in strengthening the capacity of district-level officials and promoting data-driven planning and decision-making. The technical sessions began with Ms. Palak Desai introducing the vision and objectives of the Swarna Andhra @ 2047 initiative. This was followed by an engaging session by Prof. Babbaru Venkateswarulu on the concepts of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Gross Value Added (GVA). Using simple, real-life examples, he explained the key economic concepts in an accessible manner, making the session highly interactive. The discussion soon expanded to the district's own economy, with officers actively sharing their views on Nandyal's strengths, existing challenges, and the sectors that hold the greatest potential for growth. Participants also discussed the areas that require focused attention to improve the district's overall economic performance. After the lunch break, Prof. Babbaru Venkateswarulu conducted a session on strategies to boost sectoral Gross Value Added (GVA), encouraging participants to think about practical interventions that could be implemented within their respective departments. Ms. Palak Desai then led a session on Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), which sparked an engaging discussion on tracking development outcomes and improving departmental performance through measurable indicators. The district-specific session was presented by Ms. Havila, who shared a detailed profile of Nandyal district, highlighting its economic strengths, sectoral performance, opportunities, and key challenges. The presentation received an enthusiastic response, with officers actively contributing their departmental perspectives and discussing possible strategies for improving the district's performance. The programme concluded with Ms. Havila presenting the case study of the Sahyadri Farmers Producer Company, illustrating how value addition, farmer collectivisation, and market linkages can significantly enhance rural incomes. The training concluded with closing remarks by the Chief Planning Officer (CPO) of Nandyal district, who appreciated the active participation of all departments and encouraged the officers to apply the insights gained during the programme in their future planning and implementation efforts.

points: The District Collector spoke about the tourism potential of Nandyal and how the district's resources can be used more effectively. The Fisheries Department discussed opportunities to expand fish and seaweed production, improve aquaculture practices, and achieve the district's production targets.

highlights.head: Proddatur
points: Proddatur has a two-speed profile: a rapidly urbanising Proddatur Mandal and a drought-prone agrarian Rajupalem Mandal with infrastructure gaps.
Tenant farming is a major statistical and service-delivery gap; an estimated 25-40% of cultivated area is under oral lease, while only 638 Crop Cultivator Rights Cards were issued for 2025-26.
Drought remains the dominant hazard, while PM-KISAN, crop insurance and skilling continue to face land-record and Aadhaar- linkage mismatches.

highlights.head: Kadapa
points: Only Horticulture and Fisheries submissions were available, making Kadapa the thinnest-profiled constituency in the review.
Horticulture has limited high-value perishable cropping or direct/e-NAM linkage, while inland fisheries lacks commercial shrimp culture and remains dependent on intermediaries.
Diversification is emerging through tissue-culture labs, mushroom units, nurseries, biofloc, recirculating systems and ornamental fish, but finance and post-harvest infrastructure remain constraints.

coverage: The sessions covered subnational accounting concepts (GSDP/GDDP etc), constituency economic profiles, Swarna Andhra principles findings on local strengths and constraints across Agriculture, Horticulture, Statistics and CVAP units.

highlights.head: Rajampet
points: Agriculture officers reported a shift from paddy towards groundnut, sesamum and banana due to falling groundwater, alongside strong KCC and PMFBY coverage in Rajampeta and Veeraballi.
Mango is the horticulture backbone across the constituency, with emerging diversification into dragon fruit, avocado, papaya and banana where irrigation is available.
Inadequate pack houses, grading facilities and storage are driving post-harvest losses, while produce continues to move largely through traders and commission agents.

highlights.head: Mydukur
points: Mydukur has two distinct non-farm growth engines: religious tourism around Sri Potuluri Veerabrahmendra Swamy temple and a brass-handicraft cluster of nearly 700 artisan families at Onipenta.
Brahmamgari Mattam, Duvvur and Mydukur are notified for oil-palm cultivation, while farming is shifting from paddy towards maize, bajra, blackgram, onion and turmeric as groundwater declines.
Key gaps include 15-40% post-harvest losses, absence of e-NAM or direct market linkage, saline-water damage to drip systems and incomplete linkage of resurveyed land records with Aadhaar.

points: Animal Husbandry: Kuppam has achieved full adoption of Sex Sorted Semen (SSS), while other areas use a mix of SSS and conventional methods. The department emphasized expanding SSS adoption through improved subsidies and awareness.

Fisheries: Water scarcity remains a key challenge for aquaculture. The department is promoting Biofloc and RAS technologies through pilot training programmes, with plans to scale up adoption to enhance farmers' incomes using government support.

Sericulture: Chittoor has 37,337 acres under sericulture, with Kuppam and Palamaner as major clusters, supported by two of the state's largest government cocoon markets using an online auction system. Key priorities include reducing chemical use in nearby agricultural fields and strengthening value addition through mulberry crushing machines, cocoon drying chambers, and automatic reeling machines.
Horticulture (Market & Value Addition): Limited tomato processing, challenges in obtaining INDGAP certification, and weak market linkages constrain horticultural exports and value addition.
Horticulture (Infrastructure & Productivity): Expand micro-irrigation, farm mechanization, and post-harvest infrastructure to reduce losses and enhance horticultural GVA.

Agriculture: Groundnut, the major crop in the district, is witnessing a shift towards soybean due to low groundnut yields, high seed costs, and crop damage caused by wild boars. Soybean is being promoted as a viable alternative because of its higher market value and strong demand in neighbouring districts and states.

The discussions generated valuable inputs for identifying sector-specific priorities and interventions to enhance the district's Gross Value Added (GVA).

highlights.head: Morning Session
points: Manufacturing: Mango pulp processing, valued at around ₹2,000 crore, is a key industry. Technology upgradation, affordable finance, and better infrastructure are needed to strengthen MSMEs.
Electricity: SCADA-based substation modernisation and renewable energy expansion are priority areas.

Municipal Corporation: Property tax, water charges, town planning fees, lease rentals, and advertisement taxes are the major revenue sources. Better coordination with the Tourism Department can enhance tourism promotion.
Mines & Geology: High extraction costs and outdated technology limit productivity. Modern equipment and increased mining leases can improve value creation.
Swarna Grama–Swarna Ward: Under ODOP, Terracotta is the district product but requires stronger branding and market linkages.
Roads & Buildings: Inadequate maintenance grants constrain road upkeep.

highlights.head: Afternoon Session
points: Tourism: Kaigal Waterfalls, Puligundu, Aragonda, and Gangineni Cheruvu have strong tourism potential. Improved amenities, eco-tourism, agri-tourism, and digital promotion can boost visitor inflow.
Housing: Timely project implementation depends on the availability of government land, skilled labour, and construction materials.
GST: Formalising businesses in horticulture, livestock, and manufacturing can widen the GST base.
Banking: With crop lending nearing saturation, greater focus is needed on financing food processing, value addition, and poultry-related enterprises, supported by credit awareness programmes.
Education: Greater emphasis is needed on extracurricular activities, career guidance, and future skill awareness.
Health: Preventive healthcare initiatives should focus on healthy food habits, lifestyle diseases, and cancer awareness.

highlights.head: Kuppam Constituency
points: Agriculture and allied sectors are the primary livelihood sources.
Major sectors include groundnut, ragi, paddy, horticulture, sericulture, livestock, and poultry.
Predominantly rainfed agriculture, with potential for crop diversification and strengthening FPOs.
Good scope for spiritual tourism development.
30+ industries are at various stages of establishment.
Under the P4 model, village adoption initiatives have created 17+ livelihood opportunities, supported by skill training, stipends, and employment linkages with mega and large industries.

highlights.head: Nagari Constituency
points: Agriculture is primarily based on bajra and paddy.
Oil palm cultivation is increasing, indicating changing cropping patterns and diversification potential.
Closure of the sugar factory has weakened the sugarcane ecosystem.
Scope for alternative crops, value-chain development, and diversified livelihood opportunities to compensate for the decline in sugarcane-based activities.

highlights.head: Puthalapattu Constituency
points: Strong agricultural base with high GVA potential from groundnut, paddy, mango, and horticulture, supported by tanks, and irrigation infrastructure.
Significant value-addition opportunities through 11 food processing units, with further potential in mango processing, granite, milk processing, poultry, fisheries, and MSMEs.
Growth potential in services and employment through rural tourism, highway connectivity, industrial parks, recycling units, and additional processing industries.

highlights.head: Gangadhara Nellore Constituency
points: Agriculture is driven by mango, paddy, groundnut, sugarcane, and coconut, supported by mango pulp industries; however, inadequate cold storage, drying units, and food processing infrastructure limit value addition.
Dairy, livestock, and sericulture provide significant livelihood opportunities, with coordinated fodder development and animal health programmes supporting the allied sector.
Major challenges include wild boar attacks, labour shortages, groundwater dependence, post-harvest losses, and weak market linkages.

Key interventions include strengthening FPOs, expanding processing and storage infrastructure, promoting crop diversification and climate-resilient agriculture, and leveraging tourism potential around Puligundu and other heritage sites.

highlights.head: Palamaneru Constituency
points: The constituency is predominantly rainfed, with groundnut, mango, tomato, banana, coconut, and pulses as the major crops, supported by emerging dairy and sericulture activities.
Although horticulture has strong growth potential, the absence of cold storage, pack houses, tomato processing units, and other value-addition infrastructure constrains farmers' incomes.
Key challenges include wild boar menace, labour shortages, groundwater dependence, limited agro-processing, and weak FPO capacity.

Priority interventions include establishing agro-processing and post-harvest infrastructure, strengthening FPOs and collective marketing, promoting climate-resilient crop diversification, and improving irrigation efficiency through drip irrigation.

highlights.head: Chittoor Constituency
points: Strong potential in horticulture and sericulture, supported by mango pulp processing units, cocoon reeling centres, and export- oriented mango cultivation.
Key challenges include rainfall dependence, limited assured irrigation, inadequate processing infrastructure, and weak market linkages.
Priority interventions include strengthening irrigation, promoting crop diversification and natural farming, expanding agro- processing, and strengthening FPOs and value chains.

Officials highlighted the need for greater awareness among farmers on the adverse effects of excessive pesticide usage and emphasized the importance of promoting ethical and sustainable agricultural practices.

highlights.head: Gangadhara Nellore (GD Nellore) Constituency

coverage: As part of Day 1 of the Capacity Building Programme, the District Profiling exercise focused on the Primary Sector. District-level officials from all primary sector departments participated in the session, sharing key information, sector-specific insights, challenges, and opportunities. A structured session framework, shared with participants in advance, enabled more focused discussions and the collection of high-quality inputs. The information provided by the officials was systematically documented using the WOOP (Wins, Opportunities, Obstacles, and Priorities) framework to support evidence-based district profiling and planning.

points: Tirupati district has 3,087 acres under mulberry cultivation, with around 2,500 people engaged in allied activities. Farmers cultivate FC1, FC2, and G4 mulberry varieties under the Silk Samagra-II scheme, supported by subsidies and training from the Central Silk Board and APSSRDI.

Sericulture: Major constraints include pest and disease incidence, labour shortages, inadequate infrastructure, limited crop insurance, and low youth participation. Key priorities are strengthening FPOs, expanding mulberry cultivation and irrigation, integrating sericulture with VB-GRAMG, modernizing reeling units, and improving value addition and marketing to enhance GVA.

Tirupati district has a 58 km coastline, Somasila Reservoir, 18 hatcheries, 18 prawn farms, 2 FPOs, and a 10-tonne cold storage facility. Prawns are the dominant aquaculture product and are exported through Chennai Port.

Key challenges include illegal fishing, White Spot disease, inadequate cold-chain and processing infrastructure, staff shortages, and limited institutional credit. The department emphasized expanding cold storage and processing facilities, strengthening FPOs, promoting GPS-enabled fishing boats, and improving export and marketing infrastructure.

The department is promoting Natural Farming and Integrated Farming (Agriculture + Livestock/Horticulture), particularly in rainfed mandals. Around 600 farming families receive annual support of ₹30,000, and the district has 38 Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs) and 36 trained drone pilots to support modern agricultural practices.

Agriculture: Major constraints include shortages of agricultural staff and farm labour, limited awareness of natural farming in rainfed areas, inadequate coordination at paddy procurement centres, and weak marketing facilities for natural farming produce. Strengthening extension services, market linkages, and institutional coordination were identified as key priorities to improve agricultural productivity and GVA.

The department is promoting Sex Sorted Semen (SSS) and animal-centric approaches to improve productivity; however, SSS adoption remains limited (5–10%) due to its higher cost compared to conventional insemination. To strengthen the dairy sector, 88 Mahila Dairy Cooperative Societies are targeted for establishment this year.

High input costs remain the primary challenge. As a key intervention, convergence with VBGRAMG is being leveraged for fodder development, while seven generic veterinary medical shops have been sanctioned and are currently under process, which is expected to reduce livestock input costs and improve farmers' incomes.

Mango is the district's dominant horticultural crop, with around 70,000 acres under cultivation and seven processing units. Totapuri is primarily processed, while Banginapalli is marketed for fresh consumption, making mango cultivation and processing a major contributor to horticulture GVA.

Key challenges include volatile mango prices, delayed MSP payments, low pulp recovery, and limited crop insurance. The department is promoting crop diversification, improving value addition and market linkages, and expanding oil palm cultivation from 1,200 to 2,000 acres to strengthen long-term horticultural GVA.

The department emphasized the need for stronger convergence between Forestry, Agriculture, Horticulture, and Livestock departments to improve coordination in social forestry initiatives and enhance the efficiency of afforestation and natural resource management programmes.

As a low-cost greening strategy, the department is promoting seed ball preparation and dispersal during the monsoon, including the use of drones in inaccessible forest areas. The presence of the Silviculture & Social Forestry (SS) Research Centre, Tirupati was highlighted for its role in providing technical guidance and capacity-building programmes.

highlights.head: Venkatagiri Constituency
points: Agriculture-Based Economy: Paddy, groundnut, horticulture, dairy, and sheep rearing are the main livelihood sources, supported by borewell and expanding drip irrigation. Emerging Horticulture & Natural Farming: Lime cultivation and natural farming are growing through government support and farmer groups. Infrastructure Gaps: Lack of cold storage, processing units, pack houses, grading centres, warehouses, and veterinary services limits value addition. Weak Market Linkages: Farmers depend on markets in Gudur and Karnataka due to limited local marketing and processing facilities. Growth Opportunities: Strong potential for horticulture, FPOs, dairy value addition, agro-processing, and eco-tourism in Rapur. Development Priorities: Improve irrigation, rural roads, storage, veterinary services, market linkages, and collection centres to enhance rural livelihoods.

highlights.head: Srikalahasti Constituency
points: Strong Agriculture & Allied Economy: Paddy, groundnut, millets, mango, oil palm, dairy, and livestock supported by Natural Farming, IndiGAP, and FPOs. Growing Industrial Base: Agro-processing, MSME parks, and APIIC industrial land support manufacturing and value addition. High Tourism Potential: Srikalahasti Temple, heritage sites, waterfalls, and eco-tourism offer strong tourism prospects. Infrastructure Gaps: Limited cold storage, dairy processing capacity, warehousing, export linkages, and tourism facilities constrain growth. Priority Opportunities: Expand agro-processing, dairy infrastructure, MSMEs, eco-tourism, market access, and sustainable farming.

highlights.head: Sullurupeta Constituency
points: Agriculture & Allied Economy: Paddy, horticulture, dairy, sheep rearing, and fisheries drive the economy, supported by natural farming, drip irrigation, and crop diversification. Industrial & Tourism Strengths: Tada Industrial Cluster, NH-16, proximity to Chennai, and Pulicat Lake create strong manufacturing, logistics, and eco-tourism potential. Sustainable Growth: Oil palm, dragon fruit, bamboo, dairy infrastructure, and food processing initiatives promote value addition and sustainability. Infrastructure Gaps: Limited cold storage, processing units, tourism facilities, veterinary services, skilled workforce, and market infrastructure hinder growth. Growth Opportunities: Expand agro-processing, cold-chain facilities, FPOs, dairy value addition, eco-tourism, and skill development. Development Priorities: Improve logistics, roads, sanitation, climate-resilient farming, and market linkages to boost GVA and livelihoods.

highlights.head: Sathyavedu Constituency
points: Agriculture & Horticulture: Paddy, sugarcane, mango, flowers, vegetables, oil palm, and melons drive the economy, supported by drip irrigation and crop diversification. Strong Industrial Base: Sri City, agro-processing, dairy, fisheries, and horticulture provide diversified employment and economic growth. High Export Potential: Mango pulp, flowers, fisheries, and dairy benefit from export opportunities and proximity to Chennai. Infrastructure Gaps: Limited cold chain, processing, rural roads, fisheries infrastructure, tourism facilities, and market access constrain growth. Growth Opportunities: Expand oil palm, agro-processing, FPOs, dairy, fisheries, and MSMEs while improving logistics and market infrastructure. Development Priorities: Strengthen value addition, tourism, rural infrastructure, and integrated supply chains to enhance income and GVA.

sessions.format: Virtual Constituency Profiling (Morning Session 10:15 AM to 12:50) (Afternoon Session 2.10 to 3:50)
sessions.roles: Constituencies Covered: Tirupati, Chandragiri, Koduru. CPO, DySO, Constituency Special Officers, Revenue Department (Tahsildars), Municipal Administration (Municipal Commissioners), Panchayat Raj Department (Divisional Level Panchayat Officers and MPDOs), Animal Husbandry Department (Assistant Directors), Agriculture Department (Mandal Agriculture Officers), Horticulture Department (Mandal Horticulture Officers), Statistics Department (Assistant Statistical Officers), and Young Professionals, along with the CVAP Unit
coverage: As part of Day 4 of the Capacity Building Program, the Constituency Profiling Exercise covered the Tirupati, Chandragiri, and Koduru constituencies. The Pahle India Foundation (PIF) team interacted with constituency- and mandal-level officials to understand the current status, key challenges, opportunities, and potential interventions across various sectors. The exercise was conducted in two sessions: the morning session covered the Tirupati and Chandragiri constituencies, while the afternoon session covered the Koduru constituency. The discussions generated valuable insights for identifying sector-specific priorities and formulating interventions to enhance Constituency Gross Value Added (CGVA) and Mandal Gross Value Added (MGVA).

highlights.head: Tirupati
points: Service-Led Economy: Tourism, hospitality, education, healthcare, trade, and transport are the major drivers of GVA, supported by a growing industrial and MSME base. Diversified Economic Base: Horticulture, MSMEs, logistics, animal husbandry, and upcoming industries strengthen employment and economic growth. Tourism & Human Capital: Tirumala Temple, hotels, educational institutions, healthcare, and skill development programs make Tirupati a major tourism and knowledge hub. Urban Infrastructure Development: Investments in roads, drainage, water supply, sewerage, waste management, and renewable energy are improving urban services. Key Challenges: Limited industrial land, skill and technology gaps, climate risks, water pollution, and infrastructure deficiencies constrain growth. Growth Opportunities: Expand industrial investment, strengthen tourism and MSMEs, improve urban infrastructure, promote green development, and enhance skill development to increase GVA.

highlights.head: Chandragiri
points: Horticulture-Led Economy: Mango, paddy, groundnut, tomato, vegetables, dairy, livestock, and inland fisheries form the backbone of the constituency's economy. Growing Value Addition & Tourism: Mango pulp processing, FPOs, natural farming, and heritage tourism around Chandragiri Fort create opportunities for higher income and employment. Strong Government Support: Micro-irrigation, farm mechanization, PM-Kisan, livestock development, and horticulture schemes are strengthening agricultural productivity. Key Challenges: Limited processing units, cold storage, dairy and fisheries infrastructure, groundwater depletion, and drainage issues constrain growth. Growth Opportunities: Expand agro-processing, cold-chain facilities, dairy value addition, FPO marketing, fisheries infrastructure, and heritage tourism. Development Priorities: Improve irrigation, groundwater recharge, rural logistics, skill development, and market linkages to enhance GVA and livelihoods.

highlights.head: Koduru
points: Horticulture-Led Economy: Mango, papaya, banana, and acid lime dominate agriculture, supported by natural farming, INDGAP certification, and extensive drip irrigation. Limited Water Resources: Agriculture depends mainly on borewells, with high adoption of micro-irrigation and limited paddy cultivation. Livestock Potential: Dairy and small ruminants provide important livelihoods, with support from the Sreeja Dairy network. Infrastructure Gaps: Inadequate cold storage, processing units, solar dryers, transport, and post-harvest facilities restrict value addition. Weak Market Systems: Inactive FPOs, poor market linkages, limited export infrastructure, and low awareness of government schemes constrain farmer incomes. Growth Opportunities: Expand agro-processing, strengthen FPOs, improve cold-chain infrastructure, promote crop diversification, and enhance dairy value addition. Development Priorities: Improve rural connectivity, market access, irrigation efficiency, and farmer capacity building to boost GVA and livelihoods.

sessions.format: In-person Profiling (Morning Session 10:30 to 1:00 AM, Evening Session 2.30 to 4.45 PM)
sessions.roles: CPO, GM District Industries Sector, MSMEs Participants, DD Mines, SE APSPDCL, DM NEDCAP, AEE Panchayat Raj, Superintendent Engineer RWS, Superintendent Engineer R&B, District Water Resource Officer, Project Director Housing, District Tourism Officer, Motor Vehicle Officer, Lead Bank Manager, VC TUDA, Assistant Commissioner GST, DM & HO, District SGSW Officer, Revenue Officer, MEO.
coverage: As part of Day 2 of the Capacity Building Program, the District Profiling exercise focused on the Secondary Sector in the morning session and the Tertiary Sector in the afternoon session. District-level officials from both sectors participated in the sessions, sharing key information, sector-specific insights, challenges, and opportunities. A structured session framework, shared with participants in advance, enabled more focused discussions and the collection of high-quality inputs. The information provided by the officials was systematically documented using the WOOP (Wins, Opportunities, Obstacles, and Priorities) framework to support evidence-based district profiling and planning.

highlights.head: Morning Session
points: Manufacturing: The manufacturing sector is driven by FMCG, automotive, and auto components, followed by food processing, pharmaceuticals, and engineering.

Mining: Approximately 621 acres are under mining extraction. There are 139 leases and 82 industries, including 15 granite polishing industries. The department is ahead of the target, achieving 104% revenue.

Housing Department: Affordable Housing Implementation: APS Housing Corporation is implementing *PMAY (Gramin & Urban) through Affordable Housing and Beneficiary-Led Construction (BLC) to provide permanent houses for BPL families with land, subsidies, and financial assistance. Around 26,063 houses are under construction.

Rural Water Supply (ERWS): The ERWS Department boosts rural health by providing 55 LPCD of safe drinking water, improving tap connectivity, conducting water quality tests, and implementing initiatives such as Jala Dhara–Jala Harathi, tank linkages, and water conservation.

Electricity: Discussions with APSPDCL and NREDCAP officials highlighted significant progress in renewable energy adoption and emphasized the need to expand clean energy infrastructure, improve implementation, and accelerate the district's transition to sustainable energy.

Road & Building: Officials emphasized adopting sustainable road construction methods that use recycled and eco-friendly materials to develop durable, cost-effective, and climate-resilient rural infrastructure while promoting a circular economy.

highlights.head: Afternoon Session
points: Health Department: The Health Department offers quality healthcare through 89 PHCs, 10 CHCs, and 10 labs, effectively implementing JSY, JSSK, PMJAY, NTR Vaidya Seva, e-Sanjeevani Telemedicine, ABHA ID, and EHR, enhancing maternal health and digital healthcare access.

Education Department: The Education Department emphasized strengthening quality education by improving infrastructure, welfare schemes, skill development, and awareness programs, while addressing school dropouts, parental awareness, and student well-being.

D.S.G.S.W.D. (Services): The D.S.G.S.W.D. department enhances service delivery by providing extensive citizen services through Swarna Gramam wards while prioritizing improved survey management, Aadhaar services, institutional coordination, and financial sustainability.

Tourism: Tirupati tourism centers on divine devotion, magnificent architecture, and sacred hills, anchored by the legendary Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple in Tirumala, followed by the Srikalahasti temple and Tupilipalem beach.
Transport: Drastically changed after COVID-19, with people preferring personal transport and vehicle loan approvals increasing significantly.

GST: The GST Department has strengthened transparent and efficient tax administration through AI-enabled digital systems, enhancing compliance, revenue collection, and citizen-centric service delivery.

TUDA: Tirupati Urban Development Authority emphasized strengthening urban infrastructure and addressing manpower shortages to support planned urbanization, improve service delivery, and ensure the timely implementation of development projects.

Lead District Manager (LDM): The Lead District Manager (Union Bank) emphasized strengthening financial inclusion through greater awareness of government banking schemes, financial literacy, entrepreneurship development, timely data management, and improved NPA recovery.

Revenue Department: The Revenue Department emphasized accelerating land digitization, promoting investment through IT and solar infrastructure, and strengthening urban governance to enhance service delivery and employment generation.
